analysis.summary: The small-file limit measurement (A2) stopped before it recorded any times, so we still do not know what limits fresh small-file copies after the receiver-lock change. That change was kept after 'fresh 0.411 (faster)'. xs-rs already beats rsync and xs-c++ on every lab cell, for example 9.84 s against rsync's 26.643 s on small-deep push. No other node is buildable, so the next step is to re-run A2's design (-j1 to -j16 and --no-atomic on small-deep and small-flat, both directions) to completion.

decision.reason: The A2 measurement (run 20261022T071651Z-CM-A2-10220216) ended with status 'stopped' and carries no verdicts, no times and no arm-vs-control effects, so no branch can be chosen. The lab's standing races show xs-rs at 9.84 s on small-deep fresh push against 19.878 s on pull, and 6.528 s against 9.141 s on small-flat. That confirms pull is slower, but it says nothing about how -j1 to -j16 scale, whether --no-atomic matters, or how far xs is from the receiver's local ceiling. Those are what separate path walks, per-directory requests, a saturated receiver process, writeback stalls and 'within 1.3x'. A2 stays open and the same design should be run again to completion. A measurement changes no code, so keep is false.

only fewer bytes: The compression change (c9e8d5d5f87d against 0a4953bec5d8) did not make copies faster on this link. Fresh copies were 'fresh 1.001 (equivalent)', 95% interval 0.974 to 1.030 over 8 blocks, at 12.42 s against 12.402 s. No-op re-syncs were 'noop 0.991 (inconclusive)', interval 0.942 to 1.043 over 8 blocks, at 1.714 s against 1.73 s. Eight blocks is the minimum. The fresh interval is reasonably tight around 1, but the no-op interval is wide, so this is weak evidence in both directions. The race also ran on mac-mars-usb10g, not on lab2's internet link, so it says nothing for or against the 'faster on lab2' branch. On the 10 GbE cable, where negative levels were meant to help, it bought no time. No later node depends on it. Drop it from the chain; the dictionary and long-range ideas would need a separate slow-link race.

$0.11: Re-measuring no-op re-syncs (B1) showed xs-rs ahead of rsync both ways. At -j4 it took 0.269 to 0.308 of rsync's time on real-congress and 0.231 on real-psample push. at or ahead of rsync both ways: The run's status is 'failed' and it carries no lab verdicts, so this branch rests on the arm-vs-control effects alone. Some cells kept only 8 or 9 of 10 blocks. Even so, the hypothesis that xs-rs still trails rsync on no-op re-syncs is refuted. At the default -j4, xs-rs against rsync was 0.269 (0.235 to 0.309, 10 blocks) on congress push and 0.308 (0.262 to 0.361, 10 blocks) on congress pull. It was 0.231 (0.219 to 0.245, 8 blocks) on psample push. The one weak cell is psample pull at -j4: 0.6 with a 95% interval of 0.213 to 1.689 over 9 blocks, too wide to call, at 45.418 s against 75.716 s. At -j8 xs-rs is clearly ahead in all four cells: 0.249, 0.268, 0.185, and 0.191 (0.147 to 0.249) on psample pull. -j1 is also ahead everywhere it is decided: 0.519, 0.584 and 0.421, with psample pull at 0.82 (0.317 to 2.121), inconclusive. Going from -j1 to -j8 roughly halves time on every cell, so no serial bottleneck dominates. xs-rs CPU seconds are close to rsync's at -j4 (7.747 vs 8.098 on congress push), not far above. The lab records only total CPU, not a user/kernel split, so branches 0 and 1 could not be told apart anyway, and neither is needed: xs-rs is at or ahead of rsync both ways. The remaining oddity is the high variance of psample pull at -j4 (and xs-cpp-j4 there at 2.002, 0.912 to 4.393). That is noise worth watching, not a deficit against rsync. A measurement changes no code, so keep is false.
